❓
Big Question
Today’s Wonder

Before there is a king, there is a sword in a stone. Who has the right to rule, and how would anyone know?

🎯
Objectives
By the end of this lesson…
🗺️Setting: I will find London, Winchester, Tintagel, and Caerleon on a map of Britain and name when the story takes place.
📖Reading: I will explain what the sword in the stone stands for and point to one detail that shows it.
🔤Words: I will learn five words of Arthur’s Britain.
🧵Characters: I will match facts and traits to the people of the chapter and retell it as a tapestry.
📝Writing: I will plan Quick Write 1: what makes a good knight.

🗺️ Find Arthur’s Britain
The setting: where and when the story happens

The setting is the time and place where a story happens. Start with half of the world, then zoom in. The map of Britain was drawn by John Speed in 1611 to show the island in the days of the Saxons, the time of the legend. Green names four places on the first pages of the chapter. Find each one.

🧭Tap the places Green names.
Map of Britain: John Speed, Britain as it was devided in the tyme of the Englishe Saxons (1611), public domain (source). World view: drawn for this lesson from Natural Earth map data, public domain.
3
✏️ Daily Oral Language
Study the model, then fix the sentence.
✅ Correct model
At Tintagel, the enchanter Merlin watched over King Uther.

Every name of one particular person or place starts with a capital letter: Tintagel, Merlin, King Uther. A title is part of the name when it comes right before it. Plain words like enchanter stay lowercase. Use the model to fix the sentence below.

🔧 Fix this one
merlin carried the baby from tintagel to sir ector.
Rewrite it correctly.
🔍 Check my work

Merlin carried the baby from Tintagel to Sir Ector. Three capitals: the name Merlin, which also starts the sentence, the place Tintagel, and Sir Ector, because Sir is part of his name. Baby names a kind of person, so it stays lowercase.

🪶 Poetry Corner
0 / 1

Tennyson tells the same story as Green, in verse. Here are fifteen lines from “The Coming of Arthur.” You will read more of it over the next three lessons.

The Coming of Arthur
Alfred, Lord Tennyson (1809–1892) · 1869 · the land before Arthur
0:49 AI voice
🖋️ PenTap the line that tells what changed when Arthur came.
For many a petty king ere Arthur came Ruled in this isle, and ever waging war Each upon other, wasted all the land; And still from time to time the heathen host Swarmed overseas, and harried what was left. And so there grew great tracts of wilderness, Wherein the beast was ever more and more, But man was less and less, till Arthur came. For first Aurelius lived and fought and died, And after him King Uther fought and died, But either failed to make the kingdom one. And after these King Arthur for a space, And through the puissance of his Table Round, Drew all their petty princedoms under him. Their king and head, and made a realm, and reigned.
petty: small and unimportant · ere: before · heathen host: an army of pagan invaders · harried: raided · tracts: large stretches of land · puissance: power · Table Round: the Round Table · princedoms: small kingdoms
Photograph: Julia Margaret Cameron, 1865, public domain (Wikimedia Commons)

🔤 Words: Arthur’s Britain
Five of this week’s ten words. Learn them before you read.

Say the meaning first, then tap the card to check.

⚒️
anvil
tap to flip and hear it
anvil
A heavy iron block that a blacksmith hammers metal on. A sword is stuck point down in an anvil on a stone in the churchyard.
🐎
joust
tap to flip and hear it
joust
To charge at another knight on horseback with a long lance. The knights hold a tournament and joust with lances of wood.
🧙
enchanter
tap to flip and hear it
enchanter
A person who works magic. Merlin is the great enchanter who watches over the story.
👑
sovereign
tap to flip and hear it
sovereign
A king or queen, the highest ruler in the land. After Uther dies, Britain has no sovereign, and the lords quarrel over who should rule.
⭐
destiny
tap to flip and hear it
destiny
The future that seems set for someone before they are born. Merlin says Arthur was born to great and wondrous things.

4
🎓 Questions from Professor Lovelore
She asks. You answer.
0 / 3
Professor Lovelore
Here is my first question. Many and many a man tries to pull out the sword, but not one can stir it a hair’s breadth. Then Arthur draws it out at a touch. What is Green showing you?
Your answer
Professor Lovelore
Next question. Arthur pulls out the sword because Kay needs one and the door is locked. He doesn’t even stop to read the stone. What does that show you about Arthur?
Your answer
Professor Lovelore
Last question. Sir Ector, the man who raised Arthur, kneels before him and bows his head. What does that show?
Your answer
Professor Lovelore

Well done. Now look at what your three answers have in common. The sword is never just a sword. It tests who should rule. It finds the boy who acts for others. And it makes even Sir Ector kneel.

A thing in a story that also stands for something bigger is called a symbol. The sword in the stone stands for the right to rule.

5
📖 Read like a Reader, Read like a Writer, Mimic
One sentence from the chapter, three ways.
“Without stopping to read what was written on the stone, Arthur pulled out the sword at a touch, ran back to his horse, and in a few minutes had caught up with Sir Kay and handed it over to him.”Green, The Two Swords
📖 Read like a Reader

What is Arthur thinking about in this moment, and what is he not thinking about?

✏️ Read like a Writer

The sentence is a chain of quick actions: pulled out, ran back, caught up, handed it over. Why would Green string them together without stopping? What does the speed make Arthur seem like?

🖊️ Mimic

Write your own sentence on the same pattern, about anyone or anything.

Without stopping to ___, ___ ___ ___, ___ ___, and in a few minutes ___.

You have read and noticed. Now bring the people of the chapter to life.

🧵 Stitch the Tapestry
Retell the chapter in four scenes, the way the Bayeux stitchers told their story.

The Bayeux Tapestry tells its story scene by scene, with a short line stitched above each one, and many of those lines begin with the Latin word Hic, “Here.” Build the first part of “The Two Swords” the same way. For each scene, choose what happens, stitch in the people who are there, and give them words. Type in your own words, then switch to 📜 Olde words to hear them in the voice of the old tales.

Professor Lovelore In the writer’s room

Your plan answers three questions
  1. What is one quality a good knight must have? A word or short phrase, then a few words on why.
  2. Where in “The Two Swords” does Arthur show it? A specific moment, not “he was nice.”
  3. What is one thing a good knight would never do? Something you could point to in the chapter or in your own thinking.
A few words each this week · you will draft in Lesson 3 and revise in Lesson 4
📌 Watch how
Jonah’s plan
6th Grade Scholar

Quality: Honesty. A knight who lies cannot be trusted with a sword.

Moment: Sir Kay, with his hand on the Bible, admits “My brother Arthur brought it to me.”

Never: Take credit for what someone else did.

Each line is something you could point to. The moment is a real line from the chapter, not a feeling. Notice the capitals too: Sir Kay and Arthur are names.

The moment in “The Two Swords” where Arthur shows it.
